sentenceSets.sentence: The controversy overshadowed genuine achievements that deserved more attention than the circumstances allowed.

answerChoices.reasoning: Dwarfing is a comparison of magnitude, but the sentence never says the controversy was bigger than the achievements; it says the achievements went unnoticed because of it.
To supplant is to take something's place, yet the achievements are described as still genuine and still deserving attention, so nothing replaced them.
Preempting means getting there first and crowding something out in advance, but the achievements already existed and the controversy came after them.
Negation would cancel the achievements' worth, and the sentence insists they were genuine and merited attention, so their value survives intact.
Discrediting attacks the credibility of the achievements themselves, while the sentence calls them genuine and complains only that attention went elsewhere.
Mere accompaniment would not explain why the achievements received less attention than they deserved.
Nothing is delayed here; the achievements had already been made, and only the notice given to them is at stake.
Complication implies the achievements became harder to accomplish or interpret, whereas the sentence's regret is about the attention they failed to receive.
Drawing attention to the achievements is the opposite of the outcome the sentence laments.
The sentence explicitly says the achievements got less notice than they deserved, which rules out their being honored.
Amplification would increase the achievements' prominence, contradicting the complaint that circumstances denied them attention.

sentenceSets.sentence: The new tower overshadows the small courtyard garden, and by early afternoon the roses planted there receive no direct light at all.

answerChoices.reasoning: An eclipse is a brief blocking that occurs when bodies happen to align, but the tower stands permanently above the courtyard and the effect recurs every afternoon.
Obscuring concerns what can be seen, while the stated consequence is that the roses get no sunlight, a matter of what reaches the garden from above rather than of visibility.
Engulfing implies the garden is swallowed up entirely, yet the sentence limits the effect to a particular part of the day, beginning in early afternoon.
A shroud covers something closely as a cloth would, suggesting concealment, but the tower affects the courtyard from a distance by standing between it and the sun.
Abutting describes two things touching at a boundary, which says nothing about why the roses lose their light in the afternoon.
A single tower cannot surround the courtyard, and the sentence describes one structure and one garden.
Crowding suggests the tower squeezes the garden's space, but the loss described is of sunlight rather than of room.
Blight names damage or decay directly inflicted, whereas the sentence traces the harm to the roses through the intermediate fact of lost afternoon light.
The roses are said to receive no direct light, so the tower cannot be supplying any.
Brightening contradicts the second clause, which reports the garden going dark from early afternoon onward.
Decoration has nothing to do with the sunlight the roses are losing.

sentenceSets.sentence: Growing up, he felt overshadowed by an older sister whose trophies filled the hallway shelf outside his bedroom door.

answerChoices.reasoning: Upstaging happens on a particular occasion when someone steals the moment, but the sentence describes a condition that lasted his whole childhood and a shelf he walked past every day.
Being outclassed implies the two competed and he was judged the lesser, yet the sentence never puts them in the same contest; her trophies simply sat there.
Belittling requires someone actively making him feel small, and the sister does nothing to him in the sentence except win awards.
To be sidelined is to be kept out of an activity, but he is at home in his own house, excluded from nothing the sentence mentions.
Intimidation involves fear of the other person, and the sentence gives him no reason to fear a sister whose only described act is collecting trophies.
Neglect would mean his needs went untended, while the sentence concerns how he compared with a sibling whose successes were on display.
Displacement implies he was pushed out of a position he held, but no place of his own is described as lost.
Being unnerved is a momentary loss of composure, which does not match a feeling that persisted throughout his growing up.
The sentence frames the sister's trophies as something he felt diminished by, not spurred on by.
Adoration would reverse the direction of the sentence, which reports what he suffered rather than what he gave.
Being championed means having an advocate, the opposite of the shadow the trophy shelf casts over him.
